claims.text: The fabrication baseline is powder bed fusion of CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloys using preset, fixed laser parameters without in situ feedback.
The proposed closed-loop system uses in situ melt-pool and thermal imaging to modulate laser power and scan speed in real time.
Laser power and scan speed influence the processability of LPBF CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloys.
Real-time laser modulation will improve control of melt-pool dynamics and stabilize the melt front.
A stabilized melt front will limit keyholing.
A stabilized melt front produced by parameter modulation will limit hot cracking.
Improved melt-pool control will limit uneven cooling and promote a homogeneous microstructure.
Real-time monitoring can detect deviations in melt-pool behavior and trigger corrective changes to laser parameters.
Corrective modulation of laser parameters will minimize excessive local energy input.
Excessive local energy input can contribute to fabrication defects such as hot cracking in LPBF high-entropy alloys.
The feedback system will minimize thermal gradients.
Excessive local energy input and thermal gradients are the primary drivers of dimensional deviations and defect formation.
Closed-loop builds will match the designed geometry more closely than fixed-parameter builds.
Closed-loop builds will have fewer cracks, pores, and other fabrication-induced defects than fixed-parameter builds.
Closed-loop builds will exhibit increased yield strength and tensile strength relative to fixed-parameter builds.
The predicted improvements should hold only within the calibrated operating range of the feedback system under standard LPBF conditions.
Insufficient sensor resolution or excessive feedback latency may prevent the predicted improvements.
The magnitude of improvement will depend on sensor accuracy, response time, and alloy-specific behavior.
A controlled side-by-side comparison using identical powder, layer thickness, and ambient conditions can test the effect of activating feedback.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in dimensional accuracy, mechanical performance, and defect density will falsify the hypothesis.
